Journée de la robe rouge : honorer, déno: Red Dress Day: Honouring, Denouncing, Demanding
Le sort des femmes, des filles et des pe: The fate of missing and murdered Indigenous women, girls and 2LGBTQ+ people in Canada.
5 mai 2025, près de 200 personnes se son: On May 5, 2025, nearly 200 people gathered at Cabot Square for Red Dress Day.
Parler des enjeux auxquels font face les: Talking about the issues Indigenous people face in Quebec and Canada often stirs up pain for those most directly affected. Before writing this article, I took the time to learn as much as I could, with respect and humility. Above all, I wanted to listen to those who are directly affected by these tragedies, so that their voices would be heard accurately. My intention is not to speak for them, but to relay their words.
Au square Cabot, j’ai écouté attentiveme: At Cabot Square, I listened closely to the speeches by representatives of Indigenous communities, and then spoke with demonstrators and the event’s organizers.
<strong>Ce 5 mai 2025, près de 200 perso: On May 5, 2025, nearly 200 people gathered at Cabot Square for Red Dress Day, an opportunity to remind the general public of the fate of missing and murdered Indigenous women, girls and 2LGBTQ+ people in Canada. In the crowd, the many pieces of red clothing catch the eye. The day is heavy with emotion, and tears run down some faces.
L’événement est organisé par le Projet I: The event is organized by Projet Iskweu, an initiative of the Native Women’s Shelter of Montreal. Community representatives are invited onto a stage in the middle of the square. With songs, drumming, speeches and testimonies, the mood is one of reflection.
Dans la foule, nous rencontrons Jolie-An: In the crowd, we meet Jolie-Ann, of the Anishinabe Nation, a nation in Abitibi, near Lac Simon. She is wearing a red dress, and a hand is painted over her mouth. She talks about the loss of her cousin, a tragedy that remains unsolved after all these years: “She was found on the side of Highway 117, at the entrance to Val-d’Or. The person responsible was never found. It’s going to be 22 years.”
« C’est le sentiment d’injustice qui m’a: “It’s the feeling of injustice that brings me here – to speak out about my family’s situation, but also for all the families living through this loss today,” she adds.
Les femmes qui partagent leurs témoignag: The women who share their testimonies, on stage or among themselves, are sadly used to hearing stories like this. They know these tragedies intimately. According to the Department of Justice Canada, the rate of femicide among Indigenous women and girls is 4.5 to 7 times higher each year than among non-Indigenous women. Indigenous women are also overrepresented in unresolved cases of disappearance.
Shara, une Mohawk d’Akwesasne, leur rend: Shara, a Mohawk from Akwesasne, pays tribute to them by singing on stage. A little later, visibly moved, she tells us that, like her two sisters, she has experienced sexual violence in her lifetime. “That’s why I do all this, so that my children, my nieces and my nephews don’t have to go through that.”
Partager ses traumas, les exposer, « c’e: Sharing your trauma, exposing it, “is healing, but it’s also anger,” she confides.
Dans la foule, Nahomé, de la nation anic: In the crowd, Nahomé, of the Anishinabe Algonquin nation, holds up a sign that reads, in English: “They silenced her. I speak, I fight and I remember in red.” On her mouth, the same hand painted on. She recites a poem she wrote for the occasion. “What’s important to remember on this day is that we’re still here. There are many women who are taken and never come home. Today is a day to remember all those women who have disappeared.”
Six ans se sont écoulés depuis le dépôt: Six years have passed since the release of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG). But the 231 Calls for Justice in the inquiry’s report are slow to be implemented in full. On the stage at Cabot Square, the speeches speak to the frustration caused by this wait.
Du côté du gouvernement fédéral et de l’: The federal government and the Assembly of First Nations disagree on the exact number of Calls for Justice implemented since 2019. For Senator and MMIWG commissioner Michèle Audette, creating an ombudsperson position would make it possible to track their implementation.
« Certains appels vont voir le jour, mai: “Some of the calls will come to fruition, but to me, it’s not systemic; they’re not entering the system. And that, yes, that hurts. They say it’s a matter of political will, but it’s not being made a priority,” the senator says indignantly.
Si les recommandations de l’ENFFADA pein: While the MMIWG inquiry’s recommendations are still far from fully implemented, M<sup>s</sup> Audette nonetheless sees some positive outcomes from the commission. “It’s not moving fast enough, but there are places where things are happening. Academia, for example. Lots of CEGEPs call me to come talk about the MMIWG inquiry. It’s in the curriculums, in the programs. I think that’s ‘wow’! And at the Supreme Court of Canada, it’s being used as evidence,” she says, delighted. “With all that, you tell yourself that maybe it’s gathering dust somewhere, that it’s not moving enough, but there’s a collective intelligence that means people draw examples or valuable information from this report.”
Parmi les mesures prioritaires pour la s: Among the priority measures for the safety of Indigenous women, girls and 2SLGBTQ+ people, she is calling for a nationwide public alert system for when someone goes missing. Already in place in Manitoba, the procedure works the same way as the AMBER Alert system. M<sup>s</sup> Audette tells us she will be sure to remind the new federal government of its value.
